content.thinking:
I'm thinking through the design approach for a treasure hoard prop group in a LoL-style aesthetic — exaggerated dynamic shapes, high-contrast saturated colors, glowing magic accents, readable from a high top-down camera, built as plain objects without needing a skeleton.

I'm planning the hierarchy with a root joint and a hinge joint for the chest lid, then sizing out the pieces: a hoard mound roughly 1.6m across, a chest about 0.8m wide and 0.5m tall, a crown around 0.3m diameter, goblets 0.2m tall, coins 0.04m diameter, and gems ranging 0.05-0.1m with a large glowing crystal centerpiece. I'm working out how to construct the coin mound base using a swept dome shape covered in hundreds of small merged coin discs in varying gold tones, considering whether to use painted textures or UV-mapped cylinder geometry for the coin faces.

Now I'm designing the chest itself—positioned back-left and rotated about 20° on Y, with a wooden box body painted with grain and plank lines, metal bands in a Hextech-inspired gold-and-teal palette, and high-contrast dark navy-purple surfaces trimmed in gold with glowing cyan runes and ruby gems. I'm deciding to use toon/cel shading selectively on major surfaces for readable two-tone shading mixed with gradients, and planning the chest lid as an open barrel-vault shape hinged at the back top edge, spilling glowing coins and gems from the interior.

Setting up the chest's position and yaw rotation, I'm working out how to pose the hinged lid correctly by rotating the hinge axis along with the chest's orientation, using local-to-world coordinate helpers and Euler rotations for the parts.

Rather than relying on default joint proximity, I should assign lid parts an explicit bone so they attach correctly. I'm now sketching out the element list, starting with whether the hoard needs a base plinth sitting at y=0.

I'm thinking a low octagonal stone dais with a glowing rune ring would help ground the pile visually from a top-down view, textured like dark cobblestone. Then for the gold mound itself, I'm working out a lathe profile shape that builds up from a wide base to a peak near the center.

Rather than one offset mound, I'm layering several flattened sphere domes of varying sizes to fake an off-center pile, painting them with a scattered coin pattern in base gold and darker edge tones for texture. On top, I'll scatter actual coin props across the mound surfaces with random tilted leans using surface scatter and sticking logic so they embed naturally into the pile.

For variety I'm adding standing coin stacks of varying heights built from merged octagonal cylinders, a few coins leaning or balanced on edge, and one coin rolling loose on the floor, then moving on to gem shapes cut from octahedron, dodecahedron, and lathe-based faceted forms.

I'm picking gemstone colors — ruby, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, topaz — and planning clusters of hexagonal crystal spires near the chest for a hextech-style glow effect, giving each crystal multiple tones so the glowing tip stands out while the rest keeps its faceted look instead of flattening into one solid color.

I'll use fully emissive flat-colour geometry for the crystals, building each from a mid-cyan prism body, a lighter glowing tip cone, and a near-white bright facet sliver for readability. Next I'm planning the crown: a lathed band, extruded triangular spikes with beveled tips and orbs, stuck-on gems, and a crossing arch structure.

I'm sizing the crown (0.2m diameter, 0.18m height), with dynamic alternating tall/short swept-back spikes, placed tilted on a velvet cushion near the mound apex, positioned center-front-right while the chest sits back-left. Then I'm sketching three goblets of varying design — a gem-studded lathed chalice, a tipped-over one spilling coins, and possibly a jeweled horn.

For the goblets, I'm planning painted decal patterns like filigree bands or diamond checks via a paint function, plus a silver goblet with a glowing teal liquid disc at the brim for contrast. For jewelry, I'm sweeping small gold tubes along catmull curves to create draped chains and pearl strands, adding gem pendants, a gemmed torus ring, and considering a scepter piece.

I'm keeping extras modest—a necklace, a few rings, maybe a small scroll—while skipping extras like idols or candles, and adding a spilled coin trail scattered across the dais floor. I need to stay under 1000 parts total with heavy merging, and keep flat colors under 64 while letting paints and textures handle the detail.

I'm designing a custom gold paint that blends cel shading with a gradient highlight along the surface to give it a hand-painted metallic look.

Still writing paint logic...

Now I'm planning the chest itself—dark teal/navy wood planks trimmed in gold, matching the stylized LoL aesthetic I'm going for.

Since the chest has a 15-20° yaw, I need to rotate the grain direction axis accordingly rather than using a fixed world-X direction, so I'll write a helper function to convert local directions to world space. I'll keep the chest body as a simple box with set dimensions for width, height, and depth.

For the chest itself, I'm planning an open structure with a bottom and four walls so the interior is visible, plus a squashed sphere for the gold pile peeking above the rim. The lid will be an arch-shaped profile extruded along the chest's width to form a barrel-vault shape, treated as a solid block since its inside face (visible when open) will just get a painted lining material.

Adding gold band details to the lid using an arch outline function extruded slightly larger than the lid shape, then working out similar gold strap bands wrapping the body box for visual consistency.

Then I'm planning front and side plates, L-shaped corner brackets with pointy cone accents, stubby gold feet, and base trim for a more ornate chest silhouette. For the lock mechanism, I'm picturing a shield-shaped gold plate with a glowing cyan gem and keyhole, plus rivet studs along the bands, and finally thinking through how to show the open chest's glowing interior using light-ray card textures.

Instead of soft alpha gradients, I'm switching to crisp hard-edged sparkle cards shaped like 4-point stars, scattering about 10 of varying sizes floating up to 0.9m above the hoard, keeping them double-sided and oriented to read well from the front without hanging below the floor.

I also want a ring of glowing rune decals on the dais top, placed as a flat plane just above the dais surface (y≈0.064), oriented face-up with the drawing's top pointing away from the viewer, sized to sit around the 0.8-0.98m radius band so it peeks out past the mounds covering the center.

Now I'm enlarging the dais to r=1.25 with the rune ring between 0.95-1.2m and the hoard mound extending to 0.9m, with goblets and spilled coins scattered over the rune ring. I'm working out placement coordinates for the scene: the chest sits slightly left-front at (-0.18, 0.06, -0.32) rotated about 14° to face toward the viewer's right, and a crystal cluster rises behind it around (0.35, 0.06, -0.62).

I'm placing the crystal cluster taller in the back-right at around (0.5, 0.06, -0.55) with crystals up to 0.6m to avoid overshadowing the chest, then tucking a tilted crown onto the mound's front-right at roughly (0.28, y, 0.3). I'm scattering drinkware around the hoard -- a standing gold chalice at the mound edge, a silver goblet to the right, a tipped goblet in front spilling coins, and a small cup nearby -- along with a gem cluster at front-left and a pearl necklace draped over the chest, plus coin stacks still to be placed.

To get objects to sit naturally on the lumpy mound surface, I'm defining the mounds as ellipsoid-based height functions so I can compute the exact surface height at any x,z point and raycast down onto it, since the actual faceted sphere geometry won't match a simple formula perfectly. I'm building the mounds from scaled, low-poly sphere geometry to get that faceted gem-pile look, keeping the lower half submerged.

Still working out the layout of mounds...

So the chest rim sits around 0.45 high, keeping it well clear of the mounds, and the hemisphere spheres at 14x6 should work fine for the triangle count. For the coin scatter I'm estimating around 220 small coins per mound, each an 8-sided cylinder roughly 0.032 radius and 0.007 thick, working out the triangle budget per coin.

I'm designing the coin geometry as two tiers—a rim ring plus a slightly raised inner disc in a lighter tone—to give it a more convincing coin look without going full lathe detail, and grouping tones into light/mid/deep gold variants using standard materials with scene lighting for consistency.

Flat-colored parts will read as smooth-shaded under scene lights while the cel-painted parts show banded toon shading, so I'm planning to use cel paint for the bigger objects and flat tones for merged small parts like coins, keeping the cel function driven off vertex normals in model space for anything merged.

Coins can use cel shading too since it works off normals regardless of geometry, giving nice faceted highlights on tops versus darker edges. For texel density, I'm estimating total painted area (coins plus everything else) against a paint sheet size, aiming for roughly 4mm texel resolution, and considering bumping to 2048 paintSize with a 4096 atlas for finer detail, then checking that against the snap report.

Factoring in the mounds' hemisphere surface area and the dais disc, I'm recalculating total painted area closer to 15 m², which nudges texel density toward 2.2mm at 2048 resolution. I'm now working out how cel shading applies to the curved mound geometry -- the hard shadow boundary should look fine even faceted -- and sketching a tone-mapping helper that mixes toward white for lit faces and darkens via shadow resolution for shaded ones.

Writing the cel shading function...

I'm also planning an ambient occlusion helper that darkens surfaces near the ground using a smoothstep on height, to be composed in later. Then I shift to geometry: defining a gem lathe profile with table, crown, girdle, and pavilion points, building it as a closed outline for THREE's LatheGeometry with flat-shaded segments.

For gem shading, I like how faceted lathe geometry with low segment count naturally gives per-facet cel shading through normal variation. I'm weighing an alternative approach of alternating light/dark tones per facet based on angle and height, but noting glow materials won't support that faceting well.

So I'll keep glow effects limited to a few special "magical" crystals, building them as two-part lathes (lighter crown, deeper pavilion) so the facet split still reads visually, while the rest of the pile uses non-glow cel3 shading with sparkle decals. For the scattered gem pile I'm planning to merge geometry by color group with random rotations, flat shaded, though I need to check that the lathe geometries share compatible attributes for merging.

Defining the gem profile points for the lathe...

Gem sizes range 0.04-0.09 with larger statement pieces at 0.12, and I'm sketching crystal clusters as hexagonal prisms with pointed tips using tapered cylinder geometry.

For the crystals, each one needs a body and tip part tilted outward, giving 7 crystals × 2 parts = 14 pieces. I'm layering colors from deep blue base through mid cyan to light tip, using stacked geometry bands since glow effects can't be painted as gradients directly.

For the crown structure, I'm designing a transform helper class holding position and quaternion, with methods to convert local vectors and quaternions into world space, so I can place lathes, extrusions, and spheres consistently with a slight tilt for a more natural look instead of sitting perfectly upright.

Now I'm setting up the imports for Three.js utilities, the builder, paint and texture kits, and defining the gold color palette with highlight and deep shade variants for the crown and other gilded parts.

I'm weighing deep violet-blue or teal-navy wood tones for the chest to contrast against the gold, plus a dark slate-purple dais and a cyan or ruby accent glow for the magical effect.

Settling on purple-navy wood planks with gold bands and crimson velvet lining, paired with cyan crystal highlights and a gem palette of ruby, emerald, sapphire, amethyst, and topaz for a cohesive LoL-style color scheme. Now I'm defining a toon shading function that computes lighting direction and builds a paint function for cel-shaded highlights.

Still writing shading logic...

Now I'm thinking through an ambient-occlusion wrapper that darkens colors near the ground, plus how to apply toon shading to the gold coin pile with scattered scale textures, and sketching out the lathe profile for the tiered dais base.

For the dais rim, I'm figuring out a low-poly octagonal profile for the top edge and considering a ring of small glowing cyan rune-stones set along the perimeter as decorative accents.

I'm sizing the whole prop at roughly 2.6m diameter, fitting comfortably within diorama scale, and sketching an SVG rune ring with cyan glyph strokes, triangle motifs, and gold dashed inner circle at sufficient stroke weight for clarity at render resolution.

Working out the plane scale and radii: 512 units = 2.5m, so outer circle sits around 1.22m radius, runes between 1.0-1.15m, inner dashed ring at 0.95m — checking that mound geometry doesn't overlap or obscure the visible ring area.

Now generating the 24 rune glyphs by rotating small path fragments around the circle, then listing out each gold coin mound's position, scale, and hemisphere geometry so the bases sit flush with the dais top.

I'm thinking the main coin mound could cover the chest's lower portion, letting it sit partly buried roughly 0.15 deep with the front bands still visible above the coins.

Instead I want to break the single mound into several smaller bumps placed away from the chest itself, scattered around the crown and sides so the chest remains prominent while the coins still look naturally piled. I'm plotting out the positions, radii, and heights for each individual bump.

Now I'm designing the chest's interior contents: a hemisphere dome of gold coins sitting just above the rim, plus scattered coins and gems spilling over the front edge as a separate rotated part. I'm working out the chest's local dimensions, wall thickness, and base height to fit everything proportionally.

Writing box geometry code...

Adding wood plank seam logic...

Still placing gold trim elements...

I'm positioning the lock plate on the chest's front face with slight bevel thickness, adding a small glowing cyan gem lathed into the center. Then I'm shaping the lid as a D-arch extrusion, building its elliptical curve profile across the chest width.

Writing arch outline points...

I'll settle on roughly -105 degrees for the lid rotation so the front edge swings up past vertical, with the hinge axis derived from the chest's local x-direction rotated by yaw. Then I'm working out the lid's geometry pieces, treating the arch slab's bottom face as the interior lining surface to paint with red velvet.

I'm now figuring out the gold trim bands around the lid's edges, planning a slightly enlarged outline extrusion for the border and considering sweeping a polyline along the lid's arch contour for the wrapping bands.

Thinking through orientation without the up vector...actually without specifying `up`, parallel transport should naturally keep the normal roughly radial in the YZ plane, so the default behavior should work fine even with the slight chest yaw rotation.

Now I'm planning the lid's finishing details: gold-trimmed D-shaped end caps at the box's ends, possibly a small decorative crest or studs along the top ridge, and a gold hasp tab hanging from the lid's front edge to serve as the lock tongue.

For the interior lining, I'm figuring out how to paint a quilted velvet diamond pattern using rotated 45-degree checks based on local coordinates projected onto the chest's x and z directions, with small gold stud accents placed at the pattern intersections, baked in at build-time world coordinates.

For extras, I'm adding a glowing gold dome effect inside the chest, gold coin piles, and a few faint light rays, plus a draped gold chain necklace with a ruby pendant swooping from the chest's front rim down toward the floor, built as a curved path with small radius and gold material, alongside a beaded pearl strand made of small white spheres arranged along a similar drape path.

Now I'm shaping the crown itself: a lathe-based band shell with slightly flared outer and inner radii, plus extra trim rings near the top and bottom to give it raised ridges, carefully defining the outline points so the loop closes properly without any self-intersections.

For the crown's points, I'm alternating tall and short spikes around it—exaggerated, fang-like curved shapes—each built from a tapered base that narrows to a sharp peak, extruded with a slight bevel and positioned radially around the band.

Adding ruby gems at each spike base, then alternating colored lathe gems inset into the band facing outward, oriented along the outward axis. I'm also adding two crossing arches sweeping up to a crown orb with a tiny spike, plus an interior velvet cap.

Now I'm adding a crimson hemisphere dome visible between the arches, a row of small pearls along the band's bottom rim, and working out a filigree groove pattern on the band using zigzag or diamond engraving logic.

For the crown's positioning, I'm tilting it slightly on its base of coins (14° pitch, 10° roll) so it rests naturally, and checking that its scale roughly matches a real crown's proportions. Then I start building a goblet shape via a lathe profile, defining the foot, stem, and base radii.

Now I'm working out the bowl profile—outer wall curving up to the rim, then stepping across and tracing back down the inner wall to the axis—making sure the lathe loop closes properly along the axis (x=0) rather than going negative, since the full goblet needs to stand about 0.28 m tall.

For materials, I'm planning a gold toon finish with ornament bands, plus six gems ringed around the bowl using a ring helper that places gem geometry outward-facing at each stop. I'm also adding a glowing liquid disc just below the rim, sized to fit the bowl opening, with color choices like magenta-gold for the gold goblet and possibly cyan-lime for a silver variant.

Now I'm settling on four distinct goblets: a tall gold chalice with ruby gems, a silver chalice glowing cyan with liquid, a squat jeweled gold cup with emerald accents, and a tipped-over bronze/gold goblet spilling coins. For the silver piece I'm choosing cooler toon tones with cyan accents and gold filigree rim bands, possibly built as stacked lathe rings or torus shapes for the trim.

For the tipped goblet, I'm positioning it lying on its side near the front of the dais, rim resting near the coin mounds, with a fan of about 25 coins spilling out from its mouth across the mound surfaces.

Now I'm setting up coin geometry generation: each coin gets a position, normal, and tone, with merged rim and inner-disc geometries grouped by three gold tones to keep the color palette compact.

Thinking through coin embossing, I decide to add inner discs on both faces so the coins look right when tilted, and I'm estimating the triangle count for the 8-sided rim and cap cylinders per coin.

With ~100 triangles per coin and 400 coins, that's roughly 40k — way over my 60k budget target once combined with everything else, so I simplify: just an 8-sided rim cylinder plus a flat circle decal for the raised disc on each face, bringing it down to about 48 tris per coin. Scaling that across scattered coins, stacks, and spill piles gives roughly 14k triangles total, which fits comfortably.

For stacked coins, I'll only render the inner circle decal on the topmost coin to save triangles, parameterizing an `addCoin` function with position, normal, tone, and an optional circles flag. Each stack will have coins with slight random offset and yaw, exaggerated thickness around 0.01, radius 0.04, so a 14-coin stack reaches about 0.14 height — I'll place a few of these using height-sampled base positions, then move on to scattering individual coins across the mounds.

Now I'm working out how to scatter loose coins across the mound surfaces: using a minimum distance filter, random perturbed normals for tilt, and embedding each coin slightly into the surface along its normal. I'll orient each coin using an `aim` helper quaternion applied via a matrix rather than lookAt, include some coins tilted upright like they're standing on edge, and filter scatter points to avoid flat areas with low normal.y and keep them away from the chest's footprint using a distance check from its center.

Then I'm planning to carve out an exclusion rectangle around the chest's exact footprint in local space so no coins spawn underneath it, and set up gem clusters at a few manual center points with randomized scatter around them. For heights, I'm defining a helper that raycasts downward through the combined mound and dais surfaces to find the ground y-value at any x/z, falling back to a default if nothing hits. I'm also figuring out build order (dais and mounds unioned for height lookups) and setting up the joint hierarchy -- a root "hoard" node and a hinge joint for the lid, where the hinge axis is recorded as the bone's local X direction in model space for the rig.

I'm working out that the lid's bone should point along the chest's forward direction so its local X axis roughly matches world -X, keeping it aligned with the chest's own axes, then posing the lid open with a rotation around that axis. All lid-attached parts (sweeps, extrudes, gems via b.stick) take a `bone: lid` option so they move with it, and I'm deciding to build and decorate the lid fully before applying the open pose so interior details get baked in correctly beforehand.

I'm checking that the lid's opening rotation doesn't make it too tall overall -- estimating the arched slab swings back to roughly 0.89 total height, which stays reasonable against the 0.7-height crystal cluster. For the back crystal cluster, I'm planning seven crystals of varying height and lean around a center point with a glow, and considering adding a decorative gold accent like a floating hextech ring or a clawed gold cradle of curved prongs rising from the base to grasp the main crystal for a more ornate look.

I'm settling on five curved gold prongs arcing from the ground up around the crystal's base as the cradle design, and thinking about adding smaller jeweled details like rings and a necklace amulet scattered on the coin mound for extra richness, while skipping a sword or dagger prop since it wasn't requested. For the sparkle effects, I'm generating a four-pointed star texture with concave curves in white-gold, then using the card-billboard system to scatter around a dozen of these glowing stars above the gems and chest opening, oriented so their bottom edge sits at each placement point.

Mixing vertical cross-facing cards with some flat upward-facing ones so the stars read well from both side and top-down views, plus adding the same tiny star shine effect onto the gold coins themselves. Overall I'm aiming for strong League-of-Legends-style color blocking: a dark purple dais, gold coin mound, cyan rune ring, and red velvet lining inside the chest, with the coin piles needing a cohesive gold hue treatment.

For gem variety, I'm defining a palette of ruby, emerald, sapphire, amethyst, topaz, and aquamarine, each toon-shaded with highlight facets and violet shadow shifts. I'm grouping gems by color into six clusters of roughly seven lathed gems each, keeping triangle counts efficient, and adding three larger standout faceted gems sitting on the coin piles for visual focal points.

Writing lathe gem geometry...

I'll skip adding extras like a skull or scroll to keep the chest details focused.

For variety, I could add a spilled coin pouch nearby — a violet sack with a gold tie, knotted neck, and coins scattered out, sitting toward the left-back of the scene.

Now I'm reviewing the builder API before coding it up — checking lathe options for segments and bone attachment, the part function's parameters like position, rotation, scale, and flat shading, plus extrude settings for thickness and bevel.

Writing transform helper class...

Writing build setup code...

I'm realizing that with only root and lid joints, I need to think through the nearest-joint assignment logic carefully — since the lid joint has no children, its bone segment might effectively be zero-length, which affects which geometry gets assigned to it versus the root.

To avoid ambiguity, I'll just explicitly set `bone: root` on all body parts rather than relying on nearest-joint inference, using a small wrapper object I can spread into each part definition for body parts and lid parts separately.

Now I'm sketching out the dimensions for the chest body: setting its position and yaw, defining the gold feet boxes at the base, and planning the body height span before moving into writing all the actual geometry code.

Writing chest body geometry...

Refining interior boundary checks...

I'll set the threshold to include inner faces and inner rim edges with a small margin, since rim tops get covered by gold trim anyway. For the plank paint, I'm setting horizontal seams spaced along y and defining wood tone colors.

Now I'm adding the crimson velvet lining with darker quilted diamonds, gold stud dots, and toon-shading throughout. For the chest's top rim, I'm positioning gold trim strips front and back, working out the overhang so they sit flush against the inner wall thickness without clipping outward too far.

Still positioning trim strips...

Placing spikes at the four corners tilted slightly outward, deciding they only matter visually at the front since the lid hinge at the back would interfere when closed, though it's open now so that's less of an issue.

Now I'm adding corner foot caps, then rows of studs along the straps and base trim, followed by building a shield-shaped lock plate on the front face with its own local coordinate frame.

For the lock plate, I'm defining the shield outline with a sharp bottom point, then layering a smaller inner navy shield, a glowing cyan gem, and a small keyhole beneath it.

Now I'm setting up the lid hinge at the back-top edge and extruding the arch-shaped lid slab along the local z-axis, extending slightly past the front edge for overhang.

I'm working out the lid's thickness axis and dimensions, then planning wood plank seams across the arched surface using an angular coordinate so the seams radiate outward at regular intervals.

Flat underside faces get a lining treatment, and the extruded side-end faces facing along the x-axis get gold end plates based on a slightly scaled and offset copy of the arch outline.

Working out gold end plate positions...

Actually the arch front has no vertical face since the curve meets the base directly, so a hanging tongue shield wouldn't sit naturally there — I'll skip that detail and rely on the lock plate on the body instead.

Now for the interior, I'm sizing a faceted gold dome hemisphere so it stays within the inner walls, then scattering painted gold coin shapes across its surface and adding a few gem highlights near the top, like a ruby or emerald nestled among draped coins.

I'm also draping a pearl-and-gold necklace from the dome's top, over the front rim, and down the front wall onto the mound, checking the path clears the lock plate area, and finishing it with a lathed ruby pendant in a gold setting.

Now I'm defining the crystal cluster near the base, laying out each shard's offset position, height, radius, and lean direction to form an irregular grouping of varying sizes.

Now I'm designing a gold prong cradle with 5 curved prongs rising from the base, using bezier sweeps that taper from wider at the ground to a fine point gripping the crystal near the top.

I'm also lathing a drawstring sack shape near the base, defining its outer profile with a cinched neck and flared mouth, then closing the loop with an inner profile back to the central axis to make it a solid form.

I'm adding bow tails and a stream of spilled gold coins flowing from the sack's mouth onto the floor, plus tilting the whole sack forward slightly for a slumped pose. For the material, I'm using a mottled purple fabric toon shader with a gold circular emblem decal on the front.

Now I'm placing eight small glowing rune pedestals around the dais rim, each a gold hexagonal base topped with a glowing cyan crystal shard. Writing SVG glyph paths...

Adding ring strokes and gold dashed accents...

I'm skipping dais edge runes but adding scattered gems and coins near the rim for floor-level detail, defining tone variants for the coin colors before writing the geometry helpers.

Building coin geometry with cylinder rims and circular faces positioned slightly above and below center, then setting up a function to place each coin with its position, surface normal, tone, and random spin.

For merging, I'll group geometries by tone so each group gets painted with a toon material—rims using the base coin tones and faces using a lighter inlay palette of soft yellows and blues for contrast. Then I stack them to form coin piles before moving on to building mounds.

Mounds use a scaled, noisy gold-toned surface with darkening near the base to suggest grounding and depth. Next I'm planning gem placement on top, where each gem's position, rotation, and color index get merged into color-grouped parts, starting with a lathe-based gem geometry defined by profile points.

I'm defining faceted gem shapes using lathe geometry with flat normals, adding variation between brilliant-cut and hexagonal prism forms, and grouping them by color for merging. I'll shade the facets with a toon threshold for highlights, then move on to adding sparkle effects and finalizing the overall piece dimensions.

I'm setting up typed helper functions for lathe outlines and a ring-band builder that creates diamond-profile torus shapes positioned along a transform's axis, then starting to write the main goblet-building function.

Shaping the chalice profile points...

Good, the edges stay non-crossing and the trophy cup height comes to roughly 0.3 meters, a reasonable "hero" scale. Now I'm thinking about style variants—gold with ornamentation versus a silver version with a slightly flared, wider bell profile—planning to reuse the same profile function but adjust scale factors for each variant.

I want to differentiate the silhouettes more distinctly: a tall slender profile, a flared tulip shape with a thin stem and wide flat foot, a squat cup with swept handles, and a tipped goblet reusing the tall profile in silver or bronze. For the gold variant I'm sketching out the paint logic to add ornamental bands, and setting up the lathe outline coordinates that define the cup's height profile in meters.

Now I'm working out a diamond zigzag pattern for the ornament band on the cup, plus a ring of six gem studs around the mid-cup, a small gem for the goblet's knot, a glowing liquid disc at the cup's rim, and a heap of gold coins piled as a squashed hemisphere dome over chalice A's rim.

I'm planning the four chalices' contents: A filled with gold coins, B with glowing liquid, C with a heap of gems, D with spilled coins, then mapping out their world positions, heights, and slight tilts for the uneven mounds they sit on.

Now I'm laying out the rest of the scene's coordinates — crown, necklace, chest, crystals, sack, and five gem clusters — checking each against neighbors like the crown and chest to avoid overlap.

I'm positioning the big gems and chalice: the chalice near the top right, a glowing ruby, and a sapphire tucked near a gem cluster on the left, then sketching out a couple of nearby coin stacks with their heights.

I'll add a couple more stacks and flattened torus rings lying across the coin pile with small gems fused onto them for the crown area, keeping the hoard readable from a top-down view. Now I'm moving into the actual code, starting with a height function that defines the ground surface contours.

I'm building a sparkle SVG shape with a four-pointed glow and inner circle, then setting up a card helper function for rendering flat textured meshes with flow direction and spin options, checking that the glow effect accepts mesh arrays correctly.

Now I'm setting up local coordinate helpers for the chest lid so I can map world positions to surface-local u/w/h values, then starting on a wood paint shader closure using those coordinates.

Writing the paint logic...

I realize my dot-check ordering is wrong — the gold dot condition needs to be evaluated before the line checks, since intersections should take priority over the line color. I also need to extend this logic to handle the vertical wall faces using u/w coordinates separately.

Working out the pattern coordinates for each wall orientation, I decide: for the bottom wall use (u,w), otherwise pick the horizontal coordinate based on which local normal axis dominates, paired with the vertical y-coordinate. The lid lining only applies to the bottom-facing wall, while other walls and the lid's curved end facets stay wood-colored.

Now I'm defining the wood grain material for the chest's outer faces and sketching out the dais stone material with lighter top cobbles versus darker side stone, plus a gem cluster function that scatters gems randomly within a spread radius at a height following the terrain.

I'm working out coin scatter logic using the surface API to place coins across the mounds while filtering out the chest footprint and low-lying areas, then adding a spill ring of extra coins and a few gems scattered around the dais at a wider radius.

For the tipped goblet, I'm figuring out its rotation order so the pitch and yaw combine correctly to angle its mouth outward, then positioning it at the right height above the surface based on its foot and bowl geometry.

I'm working out where spilled coins should land, fanning them outward from the goblet's mouth with increasing distance and lateral spread, using the terrain height function for each coin's resting position. Now I'm moving on to actually writing the full component code, being careful with TypeScript strictness around unused variables and vector math imports.

Setting up vector helpers and bone references...

Defining the joint hierarchy and mound placement loop with randomized scale and position for each coin pile...

Writing chest transform setup...

Adding corner spikes, merging stud geometry, and shaping the lock plate outline...

Still shaping the gem and keyhole geometry...

Now I'm positioning the crown using a local transform on the terrain surface, then building the band and spikes around it with evenly spaced angles for seven points.

I'm figuring out the spike geometry -- alternating tall and short points around the band with curved concave outlines, settling on eight spikes with alternating heights for symmetry.

Still defining spike extrusion and tip orbs...

For the crown top, I'm adding a ruby orb finial with a gold spike above the velvet cap, sizing the dome so it stays just inside the arch height. I'm placing a ring of merged pearl spheres around the base for the pearl trim, and considering a second filigree cord ring near the shoulder but may skip it.
